Field names and behaviour were checked against the official Claude Code skills docs; I could not run the example on a live install, so test it in a scratch repo first. If you keep pasting the same checklist into Claude Code ("review my diff, ranked by severity, don't edit anything"), that checklist wants to be a skill. A skill is a folder with one markdown file. Claude sees its short description all the time and loads the full text only when it is relevant or when you type its name, so a long procedure costs almost nothing until you use it. articles.body: This is the one I've been building toward. Over the last few posts we deployed Claude in Microsoft Foundry, said hello to it from code, and taught it to turn a messy support ticket into clean, structured data. All useful, all a bit back-end. Today it comes together into something you can actually hand to a colleague: a working agent, built in Copilot Studio, the low-code tool you already know, powered by Claude. articles.title: SeaweedFS vs MinIO: High-Concurrency Distributed S3 Object Storage at Multi-Petabyte Scale
articles.excerpt: SeaweedFS vs MinIO: High-Concurrency Distributed S3 Object Storage at Multi-Petabyte Scale Executive Summary & Decision Matrix Both systems expose an S3-compatible API, but they solve different proble…
articles.body: SeaweedFS vs MinIO: High-Concurrency Distributed S3 Object Storage at Multi-Petabyte Scale Executive Summary & Decision Matrix Both systems expose an S3-compatible API, but they solve different problems. MinIO is an erasure-coded, monolithic object store tuned for consistent low-latency GET/PUT at high aggregate throughput. SeaweedFS is a blob store (based on Facebook's Haystack paper) with O(1) volume-ID lookups, optional tiering to cloud storage, and a POSIX layer (FUSE + filer) bolted on top. The benchmark data below was collected on a 9-node NVMe cluster (Supermicro 1029P, dual Xeon Gold 6230R, 256GB RAM, 4× Samsung PM9A3 3.84TB per node, Mellanox ConnectX-5 25GbE), plus identical spot-instance clusters on AWS for TCO modeling.
articles.author: Snowden SAY | Deep Systems Lab

articles.title: Denoise before upscale: the ordering mistake, and why 2x is the ceiling
articles.excerpt: Most upscaling tutorials tell you to enlarge first. Do that and the model learns the compression blocks and enlarges them too, which is how you get a 4K file that looks worse than the 540p original. I…
articles.body: Most upscaling tutorials tell you to enlarge first. Do that and the model learns the compression blocks and enlarges them too, which is how you get a 4K file that looks worse than the 540p original. I built a browser upscaler while trying to rescue footage from an old phone, so this order is the one that survived testing rather than the one that reads well. The order that works Denoise → enlarge ≤ 2× → inspect at 100% → grade. Four steps, and each one fails differently when skipped. Denoise first. Compression does not add random noise, it adds regular blocks. Random grain is a property of the sensor; blocks are a property of the encoder. Feed blocks into an upscaler and you get larger, sharper blocks. Strip them first. Cap at 2× per axis.

articles.title: AI Agents Work in Demos. So Why Do They Fail in Production?
articles.excerpt: I've noticed something interesting about AI agent development. Building an agent that works in a demo is no longer particularly difficult. Connect an LLM to a few tools, give it a task, add some memor…
articles.body: I've noticed something interesting about AI agent development. Building an agent that works in a demo is no longer particularly difficult. Connect an LLM to a few tools, give it a task, add some memory, and you can get something impressive running surprisingly quickly. But take that same agent into a real environment, and things become different. Sometimes it calls the wrong tool. Sometimes it repeats an action. Sometimes it gets stuck trying to solve a problem that should have been simple. And that's where the real engineering begins. The problem isn't always the model. Quite often, it's the architecture around it. Autonomy isn't the same as reliability One mistake I see in agent design is giving the model too much control.
articles.author: Shweta Mishra

articles.body: Quick answer: There are four ways to cap what an AI agent can spend: give it a virtual card with network-enforced limits (Stripe Issuing for agents); give it a wallet with per-transaction and per-session caps (Coinbase Agentic Wallets, Natural); put a policy layer or approval gate in front of its payment tool (SpendNod, Veyra); or use x402 pay-per-call, which needs a capped wallet behind it because x402 sets no limit itself. Most teams combine a hard cap with a human approval step above a threshold. How we compared them Disclosure: Zapx Labs makes Veyra. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.
